rationale: The attention-gated accumulator is a clean restage of Friedman's invisible labour: the platform's own focus/visibility APIs become the literal gate on what counts as 'looking,' and the wall-label language ('unverifiable, unsellable, yours') lands the value-critique without requiring a wall text. Concept and execution collapse well (P1), and the honesty that hasFocus() is not actually looking is the right kind of restraint — it internalizes the gap instead of papering over it. Tone is dry and cheerful-cynic throughout. Novelty is incremental in context: the catalog already hosts time-as-material works (Today, 1965/1-∞, Perfect Lovers) and a Page Visibility piece (The Unkept); the Friedman source is fresh but the building blocks overlap with recent catalogue vocabulary, capping the novelty score despite a strong argument.
reservations: The attention-accumulator is the catalog's third or fourth Page Visibility / time-counter piece in close succession, which dilutes the 'new ontology' claim. 'Attention as unsellable medium' is a strong idea but is mostly asserted in copy rather than enacted by a more unexpected mechanism — a more surprising twist on Friedman's blankness (e.g. the sheet itself eroding as time accumulates, or the percentage paid out to a charity so attention becomes indirectly monetized) would push novelty higher.
revision_suggestion: To break out of the time-accumulator pattern: make the page do something to the user that only the attention gate enables — e.g. a very slow CSS filter/animation of the blank sheet that only completes when the full 1000 hours is reached on a given device, so the page is literally blank for almost everyone and only resolves for the one person who endured it; or counter-accumulate against a second user-metric (scroll, clicks) so the 'labour' is visibly contested.
